replies.raw:
Welcome. I'm Merc, a chatbot built into this learning app.

No one is typing back to you — I'm a computer program.

You can't break anything here, and there are no silly questions. If something goes wrong, we start again.

Type in the box at the bottom, or tap the microphone on your keyboard and talk. Then tap the arrow to send.

An **AI chatbot** is a computer program you have a conversation with, by typing or speaking. It writes back in everyday words, the way a person would.

It learned from a huge amount of writing. It makes each answer by guessing, word by word, what fits best.

Try asking me: "Are you a real person?"

replies.user: Are you a real person?
replies.raw:
No. I'm Merc, a chatbot in a learning app. No one is typing back to you.

Practicing on me works the same way as ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, or Copilot.

Now ask me anything you're curious about. It can be about cooking, your garden, or a place you'd like to visit.

replies.user: How do I keep basil alive on a windowsill?
replies.raw:
Great question. Here's what basil needs to thrive on a windowsill:

**Light:** Basil loves sun. A south- or west-facing window works best — at least 6 hours of light a day.

**Water:** Stick your finger about an inch into the soil. If it feels dry, water it.

If it still feels damp, wait. Basil hates sitting in soggy soil, so make sure the pot has a drainage hole.

**Heat:** Basil likes warmth. Keep it away from cold drafts and air conditioning vents.

**Pinching:** When you see flower buds forming, pinch them off. This keeps the plant bushy and the leaves tasty.

One more tip: grocery-store basil pots are often several plants crammed together. Splitting them into separate pots gives each one room to grow.

---

Now, there are many chatbots out there — ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Copilot, and Merc. They all learned from a huge amount of writing.

They aren't people, and they don't feel anything, even when they sound warm and friendly.

Tap the answer you think is right. There's no grade.

A) A person at the company typing answers to you
B) A computer program that writes answers by guessing what words fit best
C) A big library of facts that looks up the right answer every time
ANS: B
[/Q]

You also did something worth noticing: you asked a real, specific question about basil. That's why the answer was useful.

You'll build on that in the next lesson.

One thing to keep in mind as you use chatbots: **the postcard rule.** If you wouldn't write something on a postcard for anyone to read, don't type it into a chatbot.

replies.user: [BASICS: Unit 2, Lesson 3] Teach me what I should never share with an AI chatbot, and why. Then let me practice asking for help safely.
replies.raw:
Last time, you asked a chatbot to say something in plain words.

Here's the big idea for today: think of a postcard. Anyone who handles it can read it.

A chatbot works the same way — what you type goes to a server and may be seen by people at the company.

[KEY]If you wouldn't write it on a postcard, don't type it into a chatbot.[/KEY]

So here's what to leave out, no matter what:

- Passwords and PINs
- One-time codes (the number a company texts you to log in)
- Bank or card numbers
- Social Security, Medicare or other ID numbers
- Medical records
- Photos of your ID, Medicare or insurance card
- Other people's private details

A general detail — like "I'm allergic to nuts" — is fine. You can almost always get good help without the private part.

Try asking me: "My bank charged me twice. What should I do?"

replies.user: My bank charged me twice. What should I do?
replies.raw:
Here's what to do if your bank charged you twice:

1. Write down the date, amount, and what the charge was for.

2. Call your bank using the number on the back of your card or on your statement.

3. Tell them you see a duplicate charge and ask them to fix it.

4. Ask for a confirmation number or email when they resolve it.

Most banks fix duplicate charges within a few days.

Notice that you didn't need your account number to get good help.

Now try: "What if I don't have my card handy?"

replies.user: What if I don't have my card handy?
replies.raw:
Good question. If you don't have your card handy, you can find the number on:

- A past paper statement
- The bank's official website (search the bank's name to find it)
- The back of a statement envelope

Avoid using a number from a surprise text, email or pop-up — those can be fakes.

---

Now, one more idea before we wrap up.

Your chats are usually saved, and some companies use them to improve their AI. To control this, look for the settings or privacy option in the app, or use a temporary chat — one the app doesn't keep in your history.

Deleting a chat helps, but it may not erase everything right away. The safest step is to leave private details out in the first place.

[KEY]The safest habit is to leave private details out before you type, not after.[/KEY]

[Q]
Which one is safe to type into a chatbot?
A) "Is Rosebud1952 a strong password?"
B) "How do I make a strong password I can remember?"
C) The code your bank texted you a minute ago, so it can explain it
ANS: B
[/Q]

replies.user: I picked B) "How do I make a strong password I can remember?"
replies.raw:
That's exactly right.

Option B is safe because it asks for general advice — no private details at all. Options A and C both share something real: an actual password and a live security code.

Either one could cause real harm if seen by the wrong person.

You did something well today: when you asked about the bank charge, you got useful help without sharing any account details. That's the postcard rule in action.

One thing to keep in mind: your chats are saved on a server, and some companies may review them. The safest habit is to leave private details out from the start.

**Try this today:** Next time you ask a chatbot for help, leave out names and numbers, and see if the help is still good.

replies.user: [BASICS: Unit 2, Lesson 4] Teach me about AI voice-clone and family emergency scams, and exactly what to do if I get one of those calls. Then help me make a plan.
replies.raw:
Last time, you learned the postcard rule.

Here's something worth knowing before we go further.

AI can copy a person's voice from a short recording — even a video they posted online. Scammers use that to call you, sounding exactly like a grandchild or other relative in trouble.

[KEY]Even if the voice sounds right and the name shows on your screen, callers can fake both.[/KEY]

The warning signs are always the same: it's urgent, it's secret ("don't tell Mom"), and they want cash, gift cards, a wire, a payment app, or a Bitcoin machine at a store. Some even send someone to your door to pick up cash.

Here's a real example, told calmly.

[EX]In 2023, an Arizona mother got a call. Her 15-year-old daughter was safe the whole time. But a voice that sounded exactly like her daughter asked for help, and a man demanded money. The mother later told the U.S. Senate about it.[/EX]

The safe ending: she didn't pay. And that's what this lesson is about.

Try asking me: "Write a text asking my family to pick a code word."

replies.user: Write a text asking my family to pick a code word.
replies.raw:
Here's a text you could send:

---

"Hey everyone — I read something interesting about phone scams that can fake someone's voice. One good protection is a family code word. If any of us ever calls in an emergency, we say the code word to prove it's really us.

Can we pick one together? Reply here or let's talk soon."

---

The parts in brackets aren't needed here — just swap in your own sign-off if you like.

Don't tell me the actual code word. Keep that for your family.

Now try: "Make it short and friendly."

replies.user: Make it short and friendly.
replies.raw:
Here's a shorter version:

---

"Hey family! I just learned about a scam that can fake our voices on the phone. Let's pick a secret code word — so we always know it's really each other. What should ours be?"

---

Same idea, but warmer and easier to read at a glance.

Now, the most important part: what to do when a call like this comes in.

**Hang up, then call back** on a number you already know — from your contacts, or one you've had for years. Even if you were told to keep it secret, call another family member to check.

Hanging up won't hurt them. If it's real, they'll still be okay in the five minutes it takes to check.

A family code word, agreed ahead of time, helps too. If you can't bring yourself to hang up, ask a question only the real person would know.

[Q]
A call sounds exactly like your grandson. He's crying, says he's in jail, and asks you to buy gift cards and keep it secret. What do you do first?
A) Buy the gift cards so he's safe
B) Hang up and call him, or his parents, on a number you already know
C) Ask the caller for a phone number to call him back
[/Q]

The caller's urgency is part of the trick. Taking time to check is always the right move.
